Maidstone.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the county town of Kent
s1loc: Maidstone runs a busy visitor economy as the county town of Kent, anchored by Leeds Castle, described by Henry VIII as the loveliest castle in the world and set in more than 500 acres of parkland with its maze, grotto and Dog Collar Museum. Maidstone Museum, housed in the Elizabethan Chillington Manor, holds fine art, natural history and Japanese collections, while the medieval Archbishop's Palace and All Saints Church line the River Medway through the town centre.

The leisure and activity layer is just as busy. Mote Park, a Green Flag site of more than 400 acres, offers a boating lake, segway trails and the Mote Park Adventure Zone, while Kent Life Heritage Farm Park at Sandling brings families to its rare breeds and vintage village. Cobtree Manor Park, the Aqua Park watersports on the Medway and the indoor activity venues around the town keep operators working through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deep across the Weald. The Hazlitt Theatre stages drama and pantomime, the Tyrwhitt-Drake Museum of Carriages and the Kent Police Museum draw enthusiasts, and the River Festival on the Medway fills the summer calendar. The medieval College of All Saints, the Tudor Stoneacre house at Otham and the surrounding orchards and oast houses give the town and its villages a distinct historic character year-round.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade spread through the town centre and out to country houses across the Weald, with a guide and coach-tour scene built around Leeds Castle and the wider Garden of England. Maidstone East and Maidstone West stations and the M20 and M2 bring day-trippers from London and the coast, with the Kent Downs, Sissinghurst and the orchard country a short trip out for visitors based in the town.

Basingstoke.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north Hampshire
s1loc: Basingstoke carries a steady visitor economy across north Hampshire, with The Vyne, a red-brick Tudor mansion built for Lord Sandys, Henry VIII's Lord Chamberlain, and cared for by the National Trust in 13 acres of gardens just outside the town. The Milestones Museum recreates Victorian and 1930s streets indoors, while the Willis Museum and Sainsbury Gallery in the old town hall traces the area's past from archaeology to the modern day.

The leisure and activity layer centres on the Basingstoke Leisure Park, home to the Aquadrome with its flume rides and moveable-floor pools, an ice rink, a bowling alley and a multiplex cinema. Festival Place draws shoppers and diners across the year, while War Memorial Park, Eastrop Park and the canal-side walks at the Basingstoke Canal give families and activity operators green space close to the town centre.

Heritage and culture run through the wider district. The ruined Tudor Holy Ghost Chapel, Basing House, the Civil War siege site at Old Basing, and the Anvil concert hall, one of the finest acoustics in the country, anchor the cultural offer. Jane Austen's connections at Steventon and Chawton nearby, the Haymarket Theatre and the town's festival calendar keep guides and event venues busy across the seasons.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and serviced-apartment trade serving business and leisure visitors, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching out to the North Wessex Downs. Basingstoke station puts London Waterloo under an hour away, and the M3 and A303 funnel traffic toward the West Country, so operators here handle stopover trade as well as visitors heading for the chalk downland and country houses around the town.

Crawley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Gatwick area
s1loc: Crawley sits at the heart of a large visitor economy built around Gatwick Airport, just six miles away. Tilgate Park is the marquee local draw, a country park with Tilgate Nature Centre and its zoo, a walled garden, a lake and the Go Ape high-ropes course. The historic High Street, with the timber-framed George Hotel and St John the Baptist church, anchors a New Town that grew rapidly around its older Sussex core.

The leisure and activity layer is strong for a town this size. K2 Crawley offers a 50-metre pool, a climbing wall and bowls greens, while the Tilgate watersports centre runs kayaking, paddleboarding and raft building on the lake. The County Mall shopping centre, a large Cineworld and bowling complex, and the nearby Gatwick Aviation Museum at Charlwood with its preserved aircraft keep families and enthusiasts busy across the year.

Heritage and culture centre on The Hawth, one of the busiest arts venues in the south east, set on a 38-acre wooded site staging theatre, music, comedy and West End shows. The Worth Way and Worth Abbey, the heritage villages of Worth and Ifield with its restored watermill, and the events calendar around the town centre and Goffs Park give Crawley a cultural layer beyond its New Town reputation.

Underpinning it all is one of the densest airport-hotel clusters in the country, from the terminals out through Horley and Crawley itself, serving business travellers, stopovers and holidaymakers. Gatwick rail and the M23 put London and the Sussex coast within easy reach, and the surrounding High Weald, with Wakehurst and Standen nearby, gives visitors and tour operators a day-trip hinterland on the town's doorstep.

Chelmsford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of central Essex
s1loc: Chelmsford, the county town and a city since 2012, runs a busy visitor economy in central Essex. Hylands Estate, a Grade II-listed neo-classical villa set in 574 acres of historic parkland, is the marquee draw, long famous as the home of the V Festival. Chelmsford Cathedral, one of England's smallest, and the Chelmsford Museum at Oaklands Park, with its Marconi radio collection, anchor the town's headline attractions year-round.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. The Riverside Leisure Centre brings an ice rink, swimming pools and diving platforms, while Hylands Park, Central Park along the rivers Can and Chelmer, and the boating and walking trails through Admirals Park give families green space. Bond Street and the High Chelmer shopping quarters, a multiplex cinema and indoor activity venues keep operators trading through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run deep here as the birthplace of radio. The Marconi connection, marked at Marconi Plaza and the museum, sits alongside the Chelmsford Theatre, the Civic Theatre's successor, and the events calendar built around Hylands Park's summer festivals. The historic Stone Bridge, Tindal Square and Shire Hall, and the surrounding villages and conservation areas give the city a layered past beyond its modern centre.

Underpinning it all is a hotel trade serving commuters, business visitors and event crowds, with a guide and coach scene reaching the wider county. Chelmsford station puts London Liverpool Street around 35 minutes away, and the A12 links the city to the coast, so operators handle stopover trade as well as day-trippers heading for RHS Garden Hyde Hall and the Essex countryside on the town's doorstep.

Preston.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of central Lancashire
s1loc: Preston, a city since 2002, runs a strong visitor economy in central Lancashire. The Harris, a striking Neoclassical building of 1893, is the marquee draw, a free museum and gallery with works by Lucian Freud and Stanley Spencer and a Foucault Pendulum demonstrating the earth's rotation. The Grade I-listed Preston Guild Hall, the historic Flag Market and the Cenotaph anchor a city centre shaped by the Preston Guild tradition.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. Avenham and Miller Parks, two refined Victorian parks laid out by Edward Milner, offer a Japanese Garden, the Belvedere pavilion and riverside walks beside the Ribble, while Brockholes nature reserve, with the UK's first floating visitor village, draws families to its lakes and woodland. The Guild Wheel cycle route, indoor activity venues and the city's parks keep operators trading through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Deepdale, home of Preston North End, one of the oldest football grounds in the world, draws stadium visitors, while the Museum of Lancashire, the Lancashire Infantry Museum at Fulwood Barracks and the events at the Flag Market fill the calendar. The historic docklands at Riversway, now a marina, and the surrounding Ribble Valley give the city a layered heritage beyond its industrial past.

Underpinning it all is a hotel trade serving the city, the universities and business visitors, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching the wider county. Preston station is a key West Coast Main Line junction, and the M6, M61 and M65 meet near the city, so operators handle stopover trade as well as visitors heading for the Forest of Bowland, the Ribble Valley and the Fylde coast on the doorstep.

Walthamstow.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Waltham Forest
s1loc: Walthamstow runs a distinctive visitor economy in north-east London. Walthamstow Wetlands, Europe's largest urban wetland reserve at over 200 hectares, is the marquee draw, with its Engine House visitor centre, trails and birdlife. The William Morris Gallery in Lloyd Park, the Georgian house where the Arts and Crafts designer spent his teens, sits a short walk from the historic Walthamstow Village conservation area and the 15th-century Ancient House.

The leisure and activity layer is busy across the year. God's Own Junkyard, the late Chris Bracey's warehouse of around 1,500 vintage neon signs, draws crowds with its bar and gallery, while Lloyd Park's grounds, ponds and play spaces serve families. The Walthamstow Leisure Centre, the indoor venues of the Mall shopping centre and the watersports and walking trails out toward the Lea Valley keep operators trading through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Walthamstow Market, dating to 1885 and reckoned Europe's longest daily street market, anchors the High Street, while the Vestry House Museum, the converted Granada cinema, now the EartH and Mirth venues, and the area's festival calendar fill the events diary. The God's Own Junkyard arches, the craft breweries of Blackhorse Lane and the Walthamstow Village pubs give the area a strong creative identity.

Underpinning it all is a growing hotel and short-let trade serving visitors drawn by the area's creative reputation, with a guide and walking-tour scene built around the Wetlands and the Morris connection. Walthamstow Central on the Victoria line and the Overground put central London minutes away, and Epping Forest and the Lea Valley regional park give visitors and operators a green day-trip hinterland on the doorstep.

Basildon.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Essex
s1loc: Basildon runs a steady visitor economy in south Essex. Wat Tyler Country Park, 125 acres of meadow, scrub and saltmarsh declared an SSSI and steeped in the history of the 1381 Peasants' Revolt, is the marquee local draw, with its miniature railway, adventure playgrounds and the RSPB visitor centre. The town's New Town heritage, marked by the Brooke House and the Mother and Child sculpture in the town square, anchors a planned post-war centre.

The leisure and activity layer is lively across the year. The Festival Leisure Park, nicknamed Bas Vegas, packs in restaurants, bars, a multi-screen cinema and a bowling alley, while the Gloucester Park green space and indoor activity venues serve families. The watersports and trails at Wat Tyler, the nearby Langdon Hills country park with its commanding views, and the town's leisure centres keep operators trading through the seasons.

Heritage and culture run through the wider district. The Towngate Theatre stages drama, musicals and tribute acts at the heart of the town, while the National Motorboat Museum at Wat Tyler and the historic mill at Langdon Hills draw enthusiasts. The events calendar in the town square, the Billericay and Wickford markets nearby and the rural fringe of the Crouch valley give the area a layer of interest beyond its New Town core.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and serviced-stay trade serving business parks and visitors, with a guide and day-trip scene reaching the wider county. Basildon, Pitsea and Laindon stations put London Fenchurch Street within reach, and the A127 and A13 link the town to Southend and the Thames estuary, so operators handle stopover trade as well as day-trippers heading for the Essex coast and countryside nearby.
